questions.q: Which dialect in this course has a legacy (+) join operator alongside ANSI syntax?
options: Oracle
T-SQL
MySQL
PostgreSQL
questions.explain: Oracle is the only one of the four OLTP dialects that ever had a non-ANSI way to write an outer join; T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL have only ever used ANSI JOIN ... ON syntax.

questions.q: In 'WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id(+)', what does the (+) mean?
options: customers is the side allowed to have no matching row — equivalent to a LEFT JOIN from orders
orders is the side allowed to have no matching row
Both tables must have a matching row — equivalent to an INNER JOIN
The join should return every row from both tables regardless of a match
questions.explain: (+) marks the side of the comparison that is allowed to be missing, producing the same result as LEFT JOIN customers ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id.

questions.q: Which outer join type can (+) NOT express directly?
options: A full outer join (putting (+) on both sides raises ORA-01468)
A left outer join
A right outer join
An inner join
questions.explain: Oracle raises ORA-01468 if (+) is placed on both sides of a join condition in the same WHERE clause, so a full outer join has no direct (+) equivalent — ANSI FULL OUTER JOIN is needed instead.

questions.q: Why does ANSI join syntax hold up better than (+) once a query joins three or more tables?
options: Each join's condition stays paired with its own JOIN keyword, so the join graph stays unambiguous as more tables are added
ANSI syntax runs faster on three or more tables
(+) syntax is not legal at all once a third table is added
ANSI syntax requires fewer characters to type for large queries
questions.explain: With (+), every join condition sits in one flat WHERE clause, making it easy to apply (+) inconsistently; ANSI syntax keeps each join's logic separate and explicit no matter how many tables are involved.

questions.q: What is Oracle's own current recommendation for writing joins?
options: ANSI JOIN ... ON syntax, the same as T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
The legacy (+) operator, because it is faster
A mix of (+) and ANSI syntax chosen at random
Oracle has no join syntax recommendation
questions.explain: Even though Oracle still supports (+) for backward compatibility, Oracle itself recommends ANSI join syntax — the same syntax used across all four OLTP dialects in this course.
